transcript:
[00:00] Meeting header: 2026-03-05 08:00 PT / Duration ~62m
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Kim (Redwood SE), Rita Gomez (Redwood CSM), Laura Chen (Nimbus CTO), Carlos Rivera (Nimbus Infra), Aisha Malik (Nimbus ML)

[00:12] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. wanted to run through our edge cases demo — long context, high tps, streaming backpressure and timeouts. ethan will lead the technical walkthrough. quick intro?
[00:22] Laura: thanks Maya, yeah we are primarily curious about how Redwood performs when we feed very long conversations and when our ingestion pipeline spikes to several hundred rps. also security (VPC/KMS) is a must.
[00:35] Ethan: cool. quick agenda: 1) API + console demo for streaming and long context, 2) Optimize recommendations for batching/quant, 3) live load test to show backpressure behavior and timeouts. this will be a mix of screenshots and a short live run, small chance of flakey network.
[01:02] Carlos: that's fine, just want to see end-to-end latency percentiles under load. we expect realistic tails.
[01:12] Ethan: got it. first, quick note on naming: sometimes our internal notes say Redwood Optimize or Redwood Optiimize — disregard typos.
[01:20] (chuckle)

[01:30] Ethan: demo start — Console: show model catalog, pinned versions, and a long-context mode flag. here i load a 70k token convo (we truncated to 60k for the demo). streaming enabled. you might see prompts cut slightly in the transcription cause of the recorder.
[01:52] Laura: wait, 60k tokens? how do you maintain kv cache that big without OOMs?
[02:04] Ethan: good question. runtime uses sharded kv and slice-based cache eviction with continuity tokens. for very long contexts we recommend prefix windowing + background kv checkpointing. in practice we saw steady memory once the cache warmed — that warmup can add a few hundred ms on first large request.
[02:34] Aisha: is that automatic or do we have to manage eviction policies?
[02:40] Ethan: mostly automatic, but Optimize will recommend profiles: aggressive eviction vs keep-most-recent, and batching windows. you can pin segments for retrieval-augmented setups.

[03:05] Maya: can you show the API call for streaming?
[03:10] Ethan: yeah, here's the curl: POST /v1/generate with stream=true and we send chunked responses. client needs to handle chunk reconnects and avoid short timeouts. our SDKs have retry/backoff helpers.
[03:28] Carlos: our infra uses 15s request timeouts by default at the gateway; any guidance?
[03:33] Ethan: 15s can be risky for streaming when tokens are large — you want socket-level keepalive and per-chunk heartbeats. Redwood supports small heartbeat frames so load balancers don't kill long lived connections. if you must proxy through a gateway, set idle-timeout high or use our dedicated VPC peering to bypass LB timeouts.
[03:55] Laura: ok. what about client perceived timeouts during sustained high TPS — e.g., 500 rps with many concurrent streams?
[04:05] Ethan: two things: 1) throughput pressure triggers backpressure in the runtime — we shed work to maintain latency SLOs and we have fallback to smaller quantized variants. 2) streaming backpressure: if the server can't keep up, internal buffers fill and we either queue or drop chunks. by default we queue briefly then return a 429-like backpressure error. you can configure auto-scale/burst and per-route rate limits.
[04:40] Aisha: what's the behavior clients see? 429 immediately or delayed timeout?
[04:44] Ethan: depends — if queue fills you'll see a 429/backpressure response; sometimes proxies will produce timeouts if not configured for our heartbeat frames — that's why we recommended gateway config.

[05:10] (demo: run a short load test)
[05:20] Ethan: starting a 1-minute run: we ramp to ~400 rps sustained against a quantized 13B model pinned to dedicated nodes. watch the latency p50/p95 in the console.
[06:05] (console metrics show p50 80ms, p95 420ms, some p99 spikes)
[06:12] Carlos: seeing some p99s at 1.5s — what caused the spikes?
[06:18] Ethan: spikes usually come from cache misses and KV rehydration; also some GC on the node when tiny admin tasks run. we have trace hooks in the console to correlate requests to cache heatmap.
[06:34] Aisha: model quantization — what's the tradeoff on quality? we have fidelity constraints.
[06:40] Ethan: Optimize runs evals on your prompt set. for many tasks 4-bit quant gives small perf regression; for sensitive NLU you might prefer 8-bit or dynamic quant. we show delta metrics (perplexity, nLG) in the Optimize tab. recommend running a small eval on your real prompts.

[07:05] Laura: security: SOC2, KMS, audit logs — can you host private control plane in our VPC?
[07:14] Maya: yes, Redwood Private offers VPC-hosted control plane and on-prem packages. KMS/HSM integrations supported, plus audit logs and RBAC. we'll attach the SOC2 docs in the follow-up.
[07:26] Carlos: networking: will we need peering or transit gateway?
[07:30] Ethan: either peering or transit gateway works; for low-latency Dedicated we recommend VPC peering - we can provide a template for routes and security groups.

[07:50] (live demo continues; slight stutter in audio)
[08:10] Ethan: ok now showing streaming backpressure — i've configured a tight queue to force backpressure so you can see the 429 behavior. launching a synthetic burst.
[08:28] (burst)
[08:33] Laura: we got a couple of timeouts on our side — frontend threw gateway timeout, not a 429.
[08:38] Ethan: likely the LB or client timed out before our response. we logged a backpressure event in the console at the same time. you can see the trace: request id abc123 shows 'queue_full' then 'dropped-chunk' then server-side backpressure.
[08:58] Aisha: can we tune the client to gracefully reconnect and resume streaming?
[09:05] Ethan: yes, our SDKs support resume tokens for streaming — they try to reconnect and request missing chunks based on last sequence id. we also recommend exponential backoff. caveat: reconnect semantics depend on your idempotency model.

[09:30] Maya: quick question from sales side — what are typical Dedicated sizing for Nimbus use-case?
[09:36] Ethan: depends on model and tokens. for sustained 500 rps with 13B quantized and 2k average generated tokens you'd likely need a 4-8 GPU pool with autoscale headroom. we'll run sizing during the trial.
[09:55] Carlos: any known quirks with Kubernetes autoscaler? we've seen pods thrash with bursty loads in other systems.
[10:02] Ethan: our infra uses a custom scheduler that prefers warm pools and pre-warms kernels; autoscale adds nodes based on queue length not only CPU. reduces thrash. still recommend warm standby for bursty workloads.

[10:30] (customer asks about observability)
[10:36] Maya: Console has per-route token cost, latency breakdown, and traces to correlate prompt sets. Optimize suggests batching windows and quant profiles and estimates cost savings.
[10:48] Aisha: can Optimize recommend batch sizes per route automatically?
[10:51] Ethan: yes, it profiles your request distribution and suggests batch_size, timeout settings, and caching TTLs. suggestions show expected token/sec improvements and cost delta.

[11:10] Laura: about long-context — if we keep 100k token histories and do retrieval augmented queries, is there a recommended pattern?
11:18 Ethan: for 100k generally use RAG: store full convo in a vector db and only stream relevant segments into the model to keep KV cache small. we also support pinned segments for critical context.

[11:40] (brief pause)
[11:48] Carlos: how about troubleshooting — if we see intermittent 524/timeout, what's first thing to check?
11:53 Ethan: check gateway and LB idle timeout, then console traces for 'queue_full' events, and node memory pressure. we have a runbook we can share.

[12:10] Maya: ok let's talk next steps quickly. we'll set up a Dedicated trial: 4 GPUs, quantized 13B, two weeks. SE to run initial load test and share bench results. we'll also send SOC2 and network templates.

[12:30] Laura: sounds good. also want the Optimize eval run on our prompt set before we start heavy tests.
[12:38] Aisha: i'll upload a prompt corpus to the shared folder after the call.

[12:45] Maya: recap of actions — maya send pricing and bench sheet; ethan prepare trial config and run initial test; aisha upload prompts; carlos share IT contacts. we'll meet for a POC check-in next Thursday.

[12:58] (signoffs)
[13:05] Laura: thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[13:10] Maya: thanks, bye.

Notes about transcription: occasional missed words and mis-typed product names ("Redwood Optiimize", "kv cash"), timestamps approximate.
